# An attained convex residual-threshold program and a strict actual hinge gap

This note uses the intrinsic approximate-cover theorem in Section 7 of
`candidate 2623b39acd3d4a1d`.
It improves the finite optimization of a sufficient residual certificate;
it does not prove that its optimal error always falls below the OC budget.
The prior single-cap convex-root-threshold theorem is in Section 5 of
`candidate af89470c3209e9d8`. The new contributions
here are the attained optimal sampled convex-threshold program and the
actual strict gap from its affine-hinge restriction, used with the t-cap
approximate-cover extension. Convex thresholds themselves were already
present in that archive.

## 1. The sampled convex-majorant program

Retain the actual convex body, positive integer bases P, intrinsic dimension
q>=1, masses V_p, total M, occupied parity count k, finite original cap
family, and integer t>=1 from that theorem. For every p in P define

    e_p=min_{J: |J|<=t} H_q(C_p intersect all_(j in J) H_j^c)^(1/q).

All e_p are finite and nonnegative; each minimum is attained over a finite
collection of original cap subsets. Introduce sampled values h_p and
vectors g_p in the vector space parallel to aff(P). Minimize

    R_conv = min sum_(p in P) h_p^q                         (1)

subject to the finite linear inequalities

    h_p>=e_p,           h_p>=0,
    h_r>=h_p+g_p.(r-p)  for all p,r in P.                  (2)

The minimum is attained. Indeed the feasible set in (h,g) is a nonempty
polyhedron: a sufficiently large constant h with all g=0 is feasible.
Its projection to the h coordinates is a closed polyhedron. This follows
by finite elimination of affine variables, as proved explicitly for the
hinge epigraph program in Section 8 of the cited source. The objective has
compact bounded sublevels in the nonnegative orthant. It therefore has a
minimizer h on the closed projected feasible set, with associated vectors
g supplied by feasibility.

For any feasible pair (h,g), put

    ell(z)=max{0, max_(p in P)[h_p+g_p.(z-p)]},
             z in conv(P).                              (3)

This is finite, nonnegative, convex, and satisfies ell(p)=h_p at every
sampled base: its own plane attains h_p, while every other plane is at most
h_p by (2). Hence the attained program supplies an admissible threshold
with total error exactly R_conv.

The approximate-cover theorem now chooses at most kt original caps whose
total uncovered intrinsic mass is at most R_conv. If every original cap
has mass at most B, then

    kt B >= M-R_conv.                                    (4)

For any g>=0 with tg<=1, the sufficient condition
R_conv<=(1-tg)M gives B>=gM/k. In particular g=gamma_d is the ambient OC
factor, and g=gamma_q is the stronger intrinsic factor when desired.

## 2. Exactness among all finite convex thresholds on conv(P)

The program (1)--(2) is not merely a restricted family of convex thresholds.
Every finite nonnegative convex ell on conv(P) has its sampled values
represented by (2), even if ell itself has no finite supporting slope at
a boundary point of conv(P).

Here is the finite interpolation argument. Set h_p=ell(p). For fixed p,
the required g_p must solve

    g_p.(r-p)<=h_r-h_p  for all r in P.                   (5)

The elementary finite Farkas alternative says that (5) fails exactly when
there are lambda_r>=0 with

    sum_r lambda_r(r-p)=0,
    sum_r lambda_r(h_r-h_p)<0.                           (6)

This alternative needs no closedness assumption on the original function.
For completeness, for a finite system A g<=b, feasibility is equivalent
to b belonging to range(A)+R_+^m. This is a closed finitely generated cone.
To verify the last closedness claim, eliminate dependent generators from
any nonnegative representation by moving along a dependence until one
coefficient first vanishes. Every vector then has a representation using
a linearly independent subset. Along a convergent sequence, pass to one
fixed such subset; its coefficients converge along a subsequence because
the corresponding injective linear map has a continuous inverse on its
image. Their limiting coefficients are nonnegative. Thus the cone is
closed. Separation from it gives exactly a multiplier lambda>=0 with
A^T lambda=0 and lambda.b<0, proving the alternative in (6).

If multipliers in (6) existed, their sum s would be positive and
p=sum_r(lambda_r/s)r. Convexity of ell would give
h_p<=sum_r(lambda_r/s)h_r, contradicting the final strict inequality in
(6). Therefore g_p exists for every p, proving (2).

It follows that R_conv is the exact minimum of sum_p ell(p)^q over all
finite nonnegative convex functions ell on conv(P) with ell(p)>=e_p.
It is attained by the explicit polyhedral function (3). In particular it
is no larger than the attained affine-hinge residual value from Section 8
of the cited source. No affine sandwich between sampled concave and convex
data is assumed.

## 3. A strict improvement for actual convex fibers and actual caps

The improvement over affine hinges can be strict even on a complete lattice
base with equal positive actual fibers. Fix any integer q>=1 and put

    C=[0,1]^2 x [0,1]^q,
    P={(0,0),(1,0),(0,1),(1,1)}.

Every integer fiber has intrinsic q-volume one and M=4. Choose the two
closed ambient caps

    H_1={z_1-z_2>=1/2},
    H_2={z_2-z_1>=1/2}.

They are genuine vertical halfspaces. At bases (0,0),(1,1) neither cap
captures any point; at (1,0) the first captures the whole fiber, and at
(0,1) the second does. Thus for either t=1 or t=2 the exact sampled
residual roots are

    e_(0,0)=e_(1,1)=1,
    e_(1,0)=e_(0,1)=0.                                  (7)

The finite nonnegative convex threshold

    ell(z)=|z_1+z_2-1|

has precisely the values (7), so its objective is 2. Every admissible
threshold must contribute at least one at each of the two positive-error
bases, hence

    R_conv=2.                                            (8)

In contrast, let (L)_+ be any admissible affine hinge. Write its affine
values at (0,0),(1,1) as a,c and at (1,0),(0,1) as b,d. The positive-error
constraints require a,c>=1, and affinity gives b+d=a+c>=2. Consequently

    a^q+c^q>=2,
    (b_+)^q+(d_+)^q
       >=2[(b_++d_+)/2]^q>=2,

where q>=1 was used only for convexity of the power function. Therefore
every affine hinge has objective at least 4. The constant L=1 attains 4,
so the exact hinge optimum is 4, strictly larger than (8).

This example uses the original complete integer square, full-dimensional
continuous fibers, and exact cap traces, without unequal sampling or an
unrealizable cap array. It is an obstruction to replacing the convex
threshold optimization by an affine hinge without loss. It is not an OC
counterexample, and no claim is made that (8) satisfies every target error
budget in (4).

There is also no contradiction with the residual-root concavity on its
positive real-base support. The threshold need dominate the residual only
at integer bases. It is allowed to lie below the real residual at, for
example, (1/2,1/2); the resulting convex strict superlevel can be nonempty
but contain no integer point. The approximate-cover theorem is built to
retain exactly that arithmetic distinction.
